1.pericope_label: O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good: they wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way

schools.summary: Augustine treats the doubled Halleluia as the title, takes the earlier psalm to have been sung of Israel and this of the universal Church, suggests the repetition answers to the cry Abba, Father with one wall of the building crying each word at the corner stone, and holds that the psalm is sweeter to the experienced and was written that the people of God might know itself in it as in a mirror.

Gill argues that the gathering is neither the deliverance from Egypt, since they were then brought out of one land and not several, nor the Babylonish captivity, since they were not gathered from all four quarters, and takes it of the effectual calling and of the calling of the Gentiles, reading the hunger and thirst of the travellers as the state of souls newly convinced; Calvin teaches that human affairs are not ruled by the wheel of fortune but by God’s judgments, and carries a note analysing the double burden and comparing the psalm with the most admired pastoral poets of antiquity.

Henry takes the deliverance as temporal and applies it spiritually, observing that when troubles become extreme that is man’s time to cry and God’s time to succour; Spurgeon holds that solitude is a great intensifier of misery, that a soul without sympathy is on the borders of hell, and that a solitary way is the way of despair.

Clarke denies that the psalm has any title, the Hallelujah prefixed by some versions having been borrowed from the close of the preceding psalm, finds it sung in parts with a double intercalary burden on the authority of a bishop’s lecture, holds the author unknown and the occasion the dedication of the second temple, allows the historical returns while holding the prophecy completed only under the Gospel, and notes that the wonders are done for the undeserving children of Adam; Wesley keeps the gathering literal, into their own land.

Keil and Delitzsch open the Fifth Book of the Psalter with this psalm and match its position against the opening of the fifth book of the Law, Israel standing there on the threshold of the promised land and here restored to the soil of its fatherland; Ellicott declines to decide whether the wandering is historical or an imaginary picture, and raises a crux at the third verse, where the word for the fourth quarter means sea and should mean west, so that either an emendation is needed or the phrase belongs with the scene of the ships that follows.

debates: Has the psalm a title? Augustine treats the doubled Halleluia as its title and builds an exposition on the repetition; Clarke says flatly that the psalm has no title in the Hebrew or in any of the versions, and that the Hallelujah prefixed to some of them was most probably borrowed from the close of the preceding psalm.

Who are the redeemed gathered out of the lands? Gill rules out both the deliverance from Egypt, since that was from one land and not several, and the Babylonish captivity, since that was not from all four quarters, and takes the verse of the effectual calling and of the Gentiles; Clarke allows the historical returns under a series of kings but holds the prophecy completed only under the Gospel; Keil and Delitzsch take it of Israel restored from the lands of the exile; Ellicott declines to decide whether any historical fact is described at all.

What is the fourth quarter of the third verse? Ellicott notes that the word used is sea, which by general usage should stand for the west, leaving the compass incomplete; he reports emendations, the best of them a word meaning right hand and so south, and then asks whether the text may be right and the phrase meant literally of those gathered out of the sea, connecting it with the fourth of the four scenes that follow.
outliers: Clarke and Calvin independently describe the same responsive structure of double intercalary burdens and both credit the same critic for the observation, Calvin’s note adding that the last two burdens are separated by two verses instead of one and that the psalm may be set beside the most admired pastoral poets of Greece and Rome.

Keil and Delitzsch match the position of this psalm at the head of the Fifth Book of the Psalter against the opening of the fifth book of the Law, where Israel stands on the threshold of the promised land, redeemed there out of Egypt and here out of the lands of the exile.
Augustine makes the psalm conditional on experience, saying it is sweeter to the experienced and that it is a wonder if it can please anyone who has not learned in his own case what he hears in it.
Clarke observes that the wonders celebrated in the burden are done for the undeserving, for the children of Adam, the corrupt descendants of a rebel father.
themes: a title denied and expounded
a psalm built to be sung in parts
a compass with one point missing
solitude counted as part of the suffering
deliverance claimed by four different centuries

10.pericope_label: Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death: he brought them out of darkness, and brake their bands in sunder

schools.summary: Henry keeps the prison general and turns the description into a reason for prizing liberty, draws the morals that those who will not be counselled cannot be helped and that afflicting providences must be improved as humbling ones, observes that prisoners have time to pray who could find none when at liberty, and insists that gates of brass could neither keep God out nor keep his people in past the set time; Spurgeon turns to the record of actual prisons, tens of thousands left to sicken in suffocating sepulchres with the dread of execution as the worst of the punishment, and holds that we should prize liberty more if we knew by experience what fetters mean.

Gill reports an old paraphrase applying the passage to the Babylonish captivity and prefers to read it of prisoners in common, deprived of the company of the living and already seeming to be in the state of the dead, and at the gates of brass reports one interpreter calling the phrases hyperbolical and another applying them to the subjection of the Roman emperors to the faith of Christ.

Clarke makes the passage a similitude for the captives in Babylon, sets out the misery as a numbered list of five and the causes as a numbered list of three, and insists that the deliverance was made so as to manifest an irresistible power, the prison torn in pieces; Wesley glosses the darkness in three words as dark prisons or dungeons.

Ellicott argues the particular reference from the vocabulary, the word for contemning being an old designation for the provocation offered by the chosen people, furnishes the cell from the prisons of the ancients which admitted no light at all and quotes Virgil twice, reads the forced labour of the eastern monarchies out of two words rendered made to bend and stumbled, and notes that the subject of the thanksgiving burden must be supplied from the participle at the head of the strophe; Keil and Delitzsch read the whole strophe as one compound subject, which is why the poet begins with participles.

debates: Whose imprisonment does the second scene describe? Gill reports the old paraphrase that applies it to the Babylonish captivity and prefers prisoners in common; Clarke makes it a similitude for the captives in Babylon; Ellicott argues from the vocabulary that the verse is certainly more applicable to a violation of Israel’s covenant relations than to heathen opposition; Henry keeps it general and applies it to prisoners of any age.
outliers: Ellicott quotes Virgil twice within this scene, once on those shut in by darkness and a blind cell who never look upon the open air, and once for a picture of the shrine of war compared with the broken gates of brass.

Ellicott reads the forced labour of the great eastern monarchies out of two words, rendering them literally as made to bend and stumbled, so that the verse becomes a picture of men staggering under the work that was the usual fate of captives.

Spurgeon leaves the exposition to describe actual prisons, places fit only to be tombs in which tens of thousands have sickened and died of broken hearts, and holds the dread of sudden execution the most hideous part of the punishment.
Gill reports one interpreter calling the gates of brass and bars of iron hyperbolical, and another applying the verse to the subjection of the Roman emperors to the faith of Christ.
themes: a dungeon furnished from a Latin poet
misery set out as a numbered list
forced labour read out of two verbs
a strophe held together by participles
liberty valued by those who have lost it

17.pericope_label: Fools because of their transgression are afflicted: he sent his word, and healed them

schools.summary: Henry makes sinners fools by an argument from self-interest, since they prejudice their health by intemperance and endanger their lives by indulging appetite, writes that those who doted most on the meat that perishes are sick of it when sickness comes so that what they took too much of they can now take nothing of, and applies the healing word to miraculous cures, to regeneration and to ordinary recoveries where God does but speak; Spurgeon holds that they are fools still even in affliction and that their folly would not depart though they were brayed in a mortar, and finds the mercy in their lying near the gates of death but not yet inside the sepulchre.

Gill denies that the fools are idiots or men devoid of natural understanding and makes them immoral persons who make a mock at sin, corrects the clause to read because of the way of their transgressions and infers a settled course rather than a single act, reads the healing word at three levels as the order given to the disease, the Word made flesh and the Gospel, refuses legal sacrifices for spiritual ones, and sets one king who prayed in his affliction against another who sought only to the physicians.

Clarke corrects the received version to read because of the way of their transgressions, holds that most human maladies are the fruits of sin and that misery and sin are married in bonds that can never be broken, calls the loathing of food a natural description of a sick man whose frame death has seized, and has the healed bring the life of an innocent animal in confession that God spared them when they deserved to die; Wesley glosses the affliction in two words as sickness.

Ellicott glosses the fools as infatuated in wickedness, renders the verb properly as bringing affliction on themselves, reports the versions that have they were humbled and the reading that would make the whole scene one of grieving for sin, and rejects it because the analogy of the other stanzas is against putting repentance before the cry; he also notes that the word for soul is commonly used of appetite and prefers pits to destructions at the close. Keil and Delitzsch treat the word for fool as an ethical notion not confined to defective intellect.

debates: Are the fools afflicted, or do they afflict themselves? Ellicott renders the verb properly as bringing affliction on themselves, reports the Greek and Latin for they were humbled, and raises the further possibility that it means afflicting themselves in the sense of grieving for sin, which would account for the distaste for food in the next verse as well as sickness would; he then rejects that reading because the analogy of the other stanzas is against placing repentance before the emphatic cry that follows.

What are the fools? Gill denies they are idiots or men devoid of natural understanding and makes them immoral persons; Keil and Delitzsch call the word an ethical notion not confined to defective intellect; Ellicott glosses it as infatuated in wickedness; Henry argues from self-interest that sinners are fools because they injure even their secular good; Spurgeon holds that they remain fools in their affliction and that no pounding would separate them from their folly.
outliers: Henry observes that those who doted most on the meat that perishes are sick of it when sickness comes, the dainties they loved being loathed, so that what they took too much of they can now take nothing of.

Gill and Henry independently read the healing word at three levels, as the command issued to the disease, as the Word made flesh who healed by speaking, and as the Gospel by which souls are converted.

Ellicott prefers pits to the received destructions at the close of the healing verse, taking it either metaphorically of the depths of suffering or literally of the graves the sufferers had drawn near to.
Gill sets two kings against each other at the verse about crying to the Lord, one who prayed in his affliction and one who sought to the physicians only and not to the Lord.
themes: folly defined by conduct and not by wit
a scene that might have been penitence instead of sickness
appetite turned to loathing
one word that heals three kinds of sickness
a habit read out of a preposition

23.pericope_label: They that go down to the sea in ships: he maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still

schools.summary: Henry supplies the sociology, the Israelites dealing little in merchandise while their seafaring neighbours did, notes drily that we read of no pleasure-boat among the king’s pleasant things so that none go to sea but on business, reports the proverb that those who would learn to pray should go to sea and turns it round into a rule that those who go to sea should learn to pray, and holds that those who have the Lord for their God are never at their faith’s end though they be at their wits’ end.

Gill keeps the scene literal, ascribing the winds to God alone who holds them in his fist and brings them out of his treasures, and supplies the heathen practice behind the crying, the mariners of the fleeing prophet each calling on his own god and the Romans reckoning tempests themselves as deities with temples and sacrifices.

Clarke gives the longest note in the chapter to the storm, a vessel poised on the ridge of a mountainous wave with a valley of frightful depth beyond, and holds that no one can form an adequate idea of it who has not been at sea in such a storm; at the calm he finds sense and sound emphatically meeting in the original, and he closes with a scene from his own time, the notes sent up to ministers in sea-port towns by sailors returning thanks for preservation from shipwreck; Wesley makes the elders the magistrates and rulers before whom men should not be ashamed to speak of God’s works.

Keil and Delitzsch refuse an allegorical reading by name and hold that the psalm speaks of men who traverse the sea by calling, not as fishermen but in commercial enterprise; Ellicott judges that the poet had evidently himself been to sea, supports the storm with a line of Virgil and a long passage of Ovid, remarks that the recollection of seasickness is the best comment on these verses, renders the wits’ end as all their wisdom swallowing itself up and the reeling as a spinning round and round, and finds in the added verse at the close a clear pointer to liturgical use.

debates: Is the sea-scene allegory or observation? Keil and Delitzsch refuse an allegorical reading by name, holding that the psalm speaks plainly of men whose calling takes them to sea in commercial enterprise; Ellicott concludes from the accuracy of the description that the poet had been to sea himself; Clarke says no one can form an adequate idea of such a storm who has not been in one; Henry alone looks for the audience rather than the author, and suggests the passage was calculated especially for the seafaring neighbours of Israel.
outliers: Henry and Ellicott independently quote the same proverb about the sea and prayer, Ellicott giving it in Latin without comment and Henry reporting it and then inverting it, so that instead of those who would learn to pray going to sea, those who will go to sea should learn to pray.

Ellicott supports the storm with a line of Virgil about being lifted to heaven on the arched surge and sinking again to the shades, and with a long passage of Ovid on mountains of water that seem about to touch the stars, and then adds that the recollection of seasickness is the best comment on the verses.
Clarke finds sense and sound emphatically meeting in the original at the stilling of the storm, and renders the line as a command that the whirlwind stand dumb and the billows be hushed.

Clarke closes with a scene from his own day, the notes sent up to the minister in sea-port towns by pious sailors returning thanks for preservation from shipwreck, and asks whether that is not something of what the psalmist requires.
themes: a storm certified by men who had been in one
a proverb quoted and then reversed
wisdom that swallows itself
tempests worshipped as gods
a refrain lengthened for public use

33.pericope_label: He turneth rivers into a wilderness, and the watersprings into dry ground: he turneth the wilderness into a standing water

schools.summary: Henry states the rule that if the land be bad it is because the inhabitants are so, sets the plantations in America against the desolations of once famous countries in Asia and Europe, and draws the economics from the sequence of verbs, that lands will not serve without lodgings nor lodgings without lands, so that man’s industry must attend God’s blessing and then God’s blessing will crown man’s industry; Spurgeon keeps to the plain reversal of the springs.

Gill reaches for the salt sea of the destroyed cities and the threat that the promised land should become brimstone and salt, observes that the reverse happens still, this country and the land in America having once been waste places and now being fruitful, and takes the sowing and planting spiritually, the fields being the world and the seed the word, the vineyards the churches and young converts the tender grapes.

Clarke turns the passage into a narrative of the first colonists, who flee a land of want, are led by providence to navigable rivers and to wells they have not digged, agree for convenience and defence to build a city, sow the fields they have cleared and see their cattle multiplied, and calls it a fine picture of the first peopling and planting of that country; Wesley supplies the reason for the judgments, the punishment of sin in some and its prevention in others.

Ellicott renders the word not barrenness but a salt marsh on the authority of the Greek and Latin, calls the psalm’s dependence on certain prophetic passages indubitable while insisting the images are used differently, the prophet thinking only of the joy of returning Israel and the psalm of God intervening in the reverses even the chosen nation must expect, and notes that the construction becomes awkward where two clauses from another book are introduced; Keil and Delitzsch read the sequence as a story, prosperity drawing the envy of the tyrannical before God ends the tyranny, and answer a critic who made the turn of fortune a retrospect.

debates: What does the psalm’s language depend on? Ellicott calls the dependence on certain prophetic passages indubitable but insists the images are employed to a different end, the prophet thinking only of the joy of returning Israel while the psalm makes the point that God intervenes in the reverses of fortune which even the chosen nation must expect; he adds that the construction becomes very awkward where two clauses are imported from another book altogether.

Is the turn of fortune a retrospect or a continuation? Keil and Delitzsch report a critic who took the verse about being minished and brought low to go back into an earlier time, and reject it on the ground that the symmetry of the continuation is against it, reading the sequence instead as prosperity drawing down the envy of the powerful before God puts an end to tyranny.
outliers: Gill, Henry and Clarke all three reach independently for the same modern instance at the turning of wilderness into watersprings, all naming the plantation of America, Clarke expanding it into a full narrative of the first colonists and Henry setting it against the desolations of once famous countries in Asia and Europe.

Henry draws an economic argument out of the order of the verbs, that lands will not serve without lodgings nor lodgings without lands, and that the fields will yield nothing unless sown, so that industry must attend blessing and blessing will then crown industry.
Ellicott renders the fruitful land turned to barrenness as turned into a salt marsh, following the Greek and the Latin.
Henry states as a rule that if the land be bad it is because the inhabitants are so, and that the ground is justly made unfruitful to those who bring forth no fruit to God.
themes: a soil punished for its tenants
three commentators reaching for the same new world
industry and blessing made to wait on each other
borrowed images turned to a different use
prosperity that attracts its own destroyer

39.pericope_label: He poureth contempt upon princes: yet setteth he the poor on high from affliction: whoso is wise, and will observe these things

schools.summary: Spurgeon makes the closing verse a rule for the reader, that those who notice providences shall never be long without a providence to notice, while warning that we must observe wisely or we may confuse ourselves and others with hasty reflections upon the dealings of the Lord.

Gill keeps the register theological, God laughing at princes and having them in derision, setting them up and pulling them down at pleasure and making them contemptible to their own subjects, and builds the lifting of the poor into a ladder from a shepherd taken to be king to those poor in purse, in gifts and in spirit, set among princes and on a Rock higher than the angels.

Clarke reads the closing verses through the wars of his own lifetime, counting the millions sacrificed and asking on whose heads their blood will be found, and names the commander against whom the powers of Europe were leagued in vain until a Russian frost destroyed his veteran troops and a particular providence intervened at the last battle; at the stopping of the mouth he holds that only the mouth could do anything, and that only by lies and calumnies, and God closes it; Wesley, without such an occasion, glosses the same verses as the banishment of men who grew insolent when exalted, forced to flee into desolate wildernesses for shelter.

Ellicott closes with two literary observations, that the figure of families like a flock is borrowed from the book of Job, as other phrases in these verses are, and that the psalm ends in the style and almost in the very words of one of the prophets; Keil and Delitzsch, who opened the psalm with an essay on its place in the Psalter, print the last four verses and add nothing at all.

debates: How far may the closing verses be applied to particular events? Clarke applies them at length to the wars and the fallen commander of his own lifetime; Wesley, writing without such an occasion, glosses them generally as the banishment of men who grew insolent when exalted; Clarke himself, at the answering verse about the poor, is careful to say that the reference is probably to the restoration from captivity but that such incidents frequently occur and the verse is applicable to a multitude of cases; Gill keeps the whole in theological terms of God setting up and pulling down at pleasure.
outliers: Clarke turns the commentary into contemporary history at the closing verses, counting the desolations of two long wars and the millions of lives sacrificed, and asking on whose heads God will find their blood when he makes inquisition for it.
Wesley’s general gloss on the wandering of princes, a banishment from their own courts and kingdoms into desolate wildernesses for shelter, describes exactly the case Clarke applies the verse to.
Ellicott finds the closing verses borrowing from the book of Job and ending in the style and almost the words of one of the prophets.
Keil and Delitzsch, who opened the psalm with a long essay on its position at the head of the Fifth Book of the Psalter, print the last four verses and add no comment whatever.
themes: a psalm read through a recent war
a general gloss that fits a particular exile
poverty climbing to a rock above the angels
a mouth stopped for want of anything true to say
a commentary that ends in silence
